Ask a biologist, "What is the purpose of life?", and they may respond, "To propagate your genes." A closely related concept is that of the "selfish gene" - that a lot (but not all) of our behaviors are motivated by the innate instinct to further our own genes at whatever cost to others.

       So, you share 100% of your genes with yourself. But you only share 50% of your genes with your sibling. Thus, you will compete with your sibling in order to get better access to resources provided by your parents because serving yourself would maximize the propagate of more of your genes.

       You would share only 25% of your genes with a half-sibling, so there would presumably be even more sibling rivalry in such a case.

       I'm only looking at genes, not taking into account gazillion other variables, like family situation, closeness, age differences, etc., which may change things. But for those moments of sibling rivalry, this genetic phenomenon is at least somewhat at play.

Evolutionary psychologists explain sibling rivalry in terms of parental investment and kin selection: a parent is inclined to spread resources equally among all children in the family, but a child wants most of the resources for him or herself.
